result: The authors identified an iron-regulated ECF-transporter (LhaSTA) in S. lugdunensis. The lhaSTA operon is located within the isd locus and encodes three components: a specificity subunit (lhaS), a transmembrane subunit (lhaT), and an ATPase (lhaA). A fur-box was identified upstream of lhaS, and qPCR analysis showed that lhaS and lhaA expression increased ~21-fold and ~12-fold, respectively, in the presence of the iron chelator EDDHA, an effect that was prevented by addition of FeSO4.
evaluation: Claims C5, C21-C27 provide converging evidence from genomic analysis (C21-C23), bioinformatic prediction (C22), and experimental validation via qPCR (C24-C26) that demonstrate iron-dependent regulation of the lhaSTA operon. The presence of a fur-box and the reversibility of EDDHA effects by FeSO4 addition strongly support iron-dependent regulation.

result: The authors demonstrate that LhaS is specific for heme. Recombinant LhaS purified from E. coli grown in heme-containing LB medium showed a distinct red color and characteristic absorption spectrum (Soret peak at 415 nm, Q-band maxima at 537 and 568 nm) consistent with histidine-coordinated heme. These features were absent when LhaS was purified from heme-deficient RPMI medium. MALDI-TOF and ESI-MS analyses confirmed the presence of heme (616.1767 Da) only in LhaS samples from LB medium. The calculated heme-LhaS binding stoichiometry was 1:0.6.
evaluation: Claims C6, C29-C37 provide multiple lines of evidence including visual observation, UV-vis spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF and ESI-MS) that consistently demonstrate heme binding to LhaS. The differential binding depending on growth medium (LB vs. RPMI) and the spectroscopic characteristics are consistent with heme coordination. The stoichiometry calculation (C37) is based on appropriate spectroscopic methods.

result: The authors demonstrate that LhaSTA represents a functional autonomous iron acquisition system. In a Δisd background, only the lhaSTA-expressing strain was able to grow with heme as the sole iron source. LhaSTA expression also increased cytosolic iron levels following incubation with heme, as measured by ferrozine assay.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by growth experiments (C38, Figure 3A) and direct measurement of intracellular iron content (C39, Figure 3B). The use of the Δisd background is critical for demonstrating that LhaSTA functions independently of the canonical Isd system. The ferrozine assay provides quantitative evidence of iron accumulation.

result: The authors demonstrate that LhaS accepts heme from diverse host-derived hemoproteins including human and murine hemoglobin, human and equine myoglobin, and hemopexin, but not from hemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes. Growth assays with ΔlhaSTA mutants showed defects on myoglobin but not on Hb-Hap complexes. In the Δisd background, lhaSTA expression enabled growth on multiple hemoproteins except Hb-Hap. TMBZ staining confirmed that recombinant LhaS accepted heme from all tested hemoproteins except Hb-Hap.
evaluation: Claims C7, C42-C52 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: growth assays with mutant strains (C42-C49), biochemical assays with recombinant protein (C51-C52, Figure 4D), and experiments in both wild-type and Δisd backgrounds. The consistent pattern across different experimental systems (inability to use Hb-Hap but ability to use other hemoproteins) strengthens the conclusions. The TMBZ staining provides direct biochemical evidence of heme transfer.

result: The authors demonstrate that LhaSTA function is independent of the canonical Isd heme acquisition system. Growth experiments using the Δisd mutant expressing lhaSTA showed that LhaSTA can function in the complete absence of all Isd-associated proteins, indicating that LhaSTA does not rely on Isd-dependent funneling of heme across the cell wall.
evaluation: Claims C8 and C84 are supported by experiments using the Δisd deletion mutant (Figures 3 and 4). The ability of lhaSTA to restore growth on various hemoproteins in the complete absence of the Isd system provides strong evidence for functional independence. This is a critical control that rules out dependence on Isd components.

result: The authors demonstrate that LhaSTA allows S. lugdunensis to proliferate on human cells as sources of nutrient iron. LhaSTA expression enhanced growth in the presence of human erythrocytes and cardiac myocytes in ex vivo assays.
evaluation: Claims C9, C62-C63, and C94 are supported by ex vivo growth experiments with human cells (Figure 5). The use of both erythrocytes (hemoglobin source) and cardiac myocytes (myoglobin source) demonstrates the physiological relevance of the broad substrate range. The experiments were conducted in the Δisd background, confirming LhaSTA-specific effects.

result: The authors conclude that LhaSTA represents the first example of an ECF-transporter involved in overcoming host-induced nutritional limitation and represents a novel broad-range heme-acquisition system that expands the hemoprotein substrate range accessible to S. lugdunensis.
evaluation: Claims C10 and C64 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from all previous results showing: (1) LhaSTA is an ECF transporter (C22), (2) it is iron-regulated (C24-C26), (3) it binds heme (C29-C36), (4) it functions as an autonomous iron acquisition system (C38-C40), (5) it has broad hemoprotein substrate range (C46-C48), and (6) it enables growth on human cells (C62-C63). The novelty claim is supported by the literature review (C3, C69-C70) showing no prior examples of ECF transporters for iron acquisition.

result: The authors attempted to establish a mouse model of systemic S. lugdunensis infection but found that S. lugdunensis N940135 was unable to establish systemic disease in mice. Even at high inoculum (3×10^7 CFU/animal), mice showed no signs of infection, and organs showed low bacterial burdens approaching sterility three days post-infection. LhaSTA expression did not increase bacterial loads in organs.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by in vivo infection experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). However, the negative result limits the ability to assess LhaSTA function in vivo. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and provide a plausible explanation based on host-specific virulence factors (C59-C61, C92-C93).

result: The authors demonstrate that S. lugdunensis possesses human-specific hemolytic factors. S. lugdunensis culture filtrates lysed human erythrocytes but not murine erythrocytes, suggesting the presence of host-specific virulence factors that may explain the inability to establish infection in mice.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 and C92-C93 are supported by hemolysis assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) showing differential lysis of human versus murine erythrocytes. This provides a plausible explanation for the failure of the mouse infection model and suggests that S. lugdunensis may have evolved human-specific virulence mechanisms.

result: The authors show that deletion of both lhaSTA and isdEFL did not completely abrogate heme acquisition, suggesting the presence of additional low-affinity heme transporters in S. lugdunensis, similar to observations in S. aureus.
evaluation: Claims C28, C81-C82 are supported by growth data (Figure 1D) showing residual growth of the double mutant on heme. The comparison to S. aureus (C82) provides context from the literature. This observation is important for understanding the complete heme acquisition machinery but does not diminish the significance of LhaSTA.

result: The authors validated their findings in a second S. lugdunensis strain (N940135) that is hemolytic, demonstrating that LhaSTA-dependent usage of hemoproteins is not strain-specific.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by growth experiments in the N940135 background (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This validation in a second strain strengthens the generalizability of the findings, though the core mechanistic insights were established in the N920143 strain.

result: The authors observed that recombinant LhaS did not accept heme from Hb-Hap complexes and speculate that binding of haptoglobin to hemoglobin might increase the strength of heme binding to the protein complex.
evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by TMBZ staining data (Figure 4D), but claim C87 is explicitly speculative. The authors acknowledge that this mechanism is unclear and that such an effect of haptoglobin is not known in the literature. Additional experiments would be needed to test this hypothesis.

result: The authors infer that LhaS has high-affinity heme binding based on co-purification of heme with heterologously expressed LhaS, suggesting low off-rates.
evaluation: Claim C74 is an inference from co-purification data (C29-C36). While co-purification is consistent with high-affinity binding, the authors explicitly state they failed to determine a precise Kd by isothermal titration calorimetry. The inference is reasonable but lacks direct quantitative measurement of binding affinity.

result: The authors note that during manuscript revision, other groups published identification of heme-specific ECF transporters in streptococci and Lactococcus sakei. Despite functional similarity, the specificity subunits show little amino acid sequence similarity, suggesting independent evolutionary development, similar to cobalamin-specific ECF components.
evaluation: Claims C95-C99 appropriately contextualize the work within concurrent discoveries in the field. The sequence comparison (C97) and evolutionary inference (C98) are supported by the analogy to cobalamin transporters (C99). This discussion appropriately acknowledges the broader significance while noting the independent nature of the discoveries.

result: The authors provide background on ECF transporters as trace nutrient acquisition systems with high-affinity substrate binding components, noting that involvement in iron acquisition was previously unknown.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C11-C12 represent established knowledge about ECF transporters supported by appropriate citations (Erkens et al., 2012; Rempel et al., 2019). Claim C3 accurately describes the knowledge gap that motivated the study.

result: The authors provide background on nutritional immunity, describing how host-induced iron limitation limits bacterial proliferation and how heme represents a rich iron source that pathogens can access.
evaluation: Claims C4, C13-C16 represent established knowledge about nutritional immunity supported by appropriate citations. This background appropriately contextualizes the biological significance of the study.

result: The authors provide background on S. lugdunensis as an unusually virulent coagulase-negative staphylococcus associated with infectious endocarditis and encoding an Isd heme acquisition system.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 represent established knowledge about S. lugdunensis supported by appropriate citations. This background establishes the clinical relevance and provides context for why this organism is of interest.

result: The authors provide extensive background on bacterial iron acquisition systems, including siderophores, Isd systems, ECF transporters, and hemophores, drawing comparisons between different bacterial species and mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C65-C91 represent literature review and established knowledge supported by appropriate citations throughout. This background appropriately contextualizes the novelty and significance of the findings within the broader field of bacterial iron acquisition.
